title: Ready to Learn: Notice, Think, Explain
subject: routines

blocks.title: Welcome, class.
lines: Sit in your place.
Put your bag under your desk.
Think about the question.

blocks.title: What helps you learn?
lines: Choose one. Be ready to explain.
blocks.footnote: Different answers are welcome.

blocks.title: Start the task, or ask for help.
lines: You do not have to get every answer right.

blocks.title: Tell your partner one thing that helps you learn.
lines: Take turns.

blocks.title: When the signal appears:
lines: Finish your sentence.
Pause.
Listen.

blocks.title: When the signal appears:
lines: Finish your sentence.
Pause.
Listen.

blocks.title: Observation
lines: What the picture shows.
There is a puddle.

blocks.title: Inference
lines: A possible explanation.
It may have rained.

blocks.title: An inference needs evidence.
lines: It might still be wrong.

blocks.title: Could the puddle have another explanation?
Someone may have spilled water.
lines: That is another possible explanation.

blocks.title: Find two things you can see.
lines: I can see…

blocks.title: Share your observations.
lines: Suggest one possible explanation.
I think… because…

blocks.title: Do we see it, or are we explaining it?
lines: One person speaks.
Others listen.

blocks.title: What is the mistake?
lines: “There is a puddle, so it definitely rained.”

blocks.title: Rain is only one possible explanation.
One possible response
lines: Other sensible explanations are welcome.
There is a puddle. It may have rained, but the water could have come from somewhere else.

blocks.title: One observation I made was…
lines: Think first. Then share when invited.

questions.prompt: There is a puddle on the path.
questions.model: We can see the puddle.

questions.prompt: It rained earlier.
questions.model: Rain is a possible explanation, but the picture does not prove it.

questions.prompt: The bench is beside the tree.
questions.model: We can see where the bench is.

questions.prompt: Someone left the umbrella behind.
questions.model: We can see the umbrella, but we do not know why it is there.

questions.prompt: There are no people in the picture.
questions.model: No people are shown.

questions.prompt: The school is closed today.
questions.model: An empty picture does not prove that the school is closed.

sections.title: Prepare with a short revision routine

blocks.title: Retrieval beats rereading
lines: Read the notes from your recent lessons. Close them and explain three ideas from memory.
Practise a question, check the explanation, and correct your reasoning.
Revisit the topics you found difficult tomorrow.
This is revision practice from teaching lessons, not an assessment paper or an answer key.

title: From product to global supply chain
subject: global-perspectives

blocks.title: Follow a T-shirt
lines: Write the four stages in order. Use the picture to check.
Tell your partner which stage needs fabric, and why.
1. Country A: grow cotton. A farmer needs water and land.
2. Country B: weave fabric. A weaver needs cotton and a loom.
3. Country C: sew the shirt. A garment worker needs fabric and a sewing machine.
4. Country D: sell the shirt. A shop worker needs finished shirts and a shop.

blocks.title: Build an explanation
lines: A supply chain links stages of production, not just places on a map.
Say: “I think … because the source says … But we do not know …”

blocks.title: Explain one connection
lines: The garment worker in C needs fabric from B to sew a shirt.
Without fabric, sewing may have to wait. “May” shows a possible effect, not a proven fact.
Now explain a different link yourself. Your partner points to the evidence.
1. Country A: grow cotton. A farmer needs water and land.
2. Country B: weave fabric. A weaver needs cotton and a loom.
3. Country C: sew the shirt. A garment worker needs fabric and a sewing machine.
4. Country D: sell the shirt. A shop worker needs finished shirts and a shop.

questions.prompt: Which briefing is most defensible?

options.label: Compare options, explain priorities and trial monitoring.
Ignore comfort because it is not money.

questions.model: A defensible recommendation acknowledges both constraints and uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Why might the revision work better?

options.label: It guarantees nobody will ever fall.
It makes expected behaviour clearer and allows support.
It removes the need to explain the rule.
It is fair only if everyone has identical needs.

questions.model: Clear behaviour and an accessible support route make the purpose easier to apply.

questions.prompt: Which response considers competing perspectives?

options.label: Give all space to the loudest group.
Assume every pupil wants the same activity.
Compare access needs and test a timetable with feedback.

questions.model: The response recognises access and competing uses without assuming a uniform preference.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is supported?

options.label: The cyclist certainly broke the gate.
The loose hinge proves nobody touched the gate.
The most shared post is the best evidence.

questions.model: Neither proximity nor a prior fault establishes the cause of this event.

questions.prompt: Which addition strengthens the reasoning most?

options.label: Check staffing and repeat the count before a trial.
Repeat the claim in larger letters.
Replace the count with an unrelated sports result.

questions.model: It tests whether the proposed response is feasible and the observed demand is typical.

questions.prompt: Which next step is most reasonable?

options.label: Check permission and repeat observations before a low-cost trial.
Treat one afternoon as a complete safety study.
Promise that signs eliminate every risk.

questions.model: A trial can fit the budget, but permission and stronger evidence are needed.

questions.prompt: Which agreement can we test?

options.label: Label the layout, times, duties and review checks.

cards.back: A briefing joins evidence, criteria, uncertainty and an actionable next step.

questions.prompt: Which next step is strongest?

options.label: Claim B is proven before testing.
Require every pupil to buy a device.
Trial a clear policy with offline access and evaluate results.
Allow unverified citations if they look professional.

questions.model: A trial can compare outcomes while addressing access and evidence limits.

questions.prompt: Which question captures the connections?

options.label: Why is parking always the only solution?
Can one opinion prove everyone's needs?
How would parking changes affect travel, trade and access to green space?

questions.model: The question keeps multiple effects and perspectives open to investigation.

questions.prompt: Which summary is fair?

options.label: Several groups value access but experience it differently.
People who live there never use shops.
The planner has proved the proposal will work.

questions.model: The statements find overlapping goals without inventing beliefs.

questions.prompt: Which statement is accurate?

options.label: Bus time fell 25%; car time rose 3 minutes.
The trial proves weather had no effect.

questions.model: The bus change is 10/40 = 25%; an average does not describe every trip.

questions.prompt: Which improvement is most appropriate?

options.label: Collect names to make the sample larger.
Stand in traffic for a better view.
Repeat anonymous counts at agreed times with permission.
Generalise one count to the whole year.

questions.model: Repeated safe, anonymous observations improve coverage without unnecessary personal data.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is most defensible?

options.label: Choose shelter solely because it is cheaper.
Consider need and impact as well as users per cost.

questions.model: User counts and cost matter, but do not capture safety or inclusion on their own.

questions.prompt: Which claim can the consultation support?

options.label: 60 out of 95 people who live there prefer shelter.
Most people in Bishkek want this exact design.
These people who answered raised several needs; overlap and missing voices need checking.
The largest request count settles the fairest design.

questions.model: The requests are voluntary and may overlap. They find needs in this consultation without establishing population shares or a fair final design.

questions.prompt: Which field note is checkable?
lines:

Example B: The room was popular.

questions.prompt: Does a long queue prove that service is slow?
questions.model: No. More arrivals could also increase the queue; count and time what happens.

questions.prompt: A queue is longer at Gate X. What can a single count establish?
lines: A queue is longer at Gate X. What can a single count establish?
questions.model: More people were waiting there at that moment. A snapshot describes a moment; repeated timing would be needed to compare service.

questions.prompt: Which change improves a fair comparison?
lines:
Which change improves a fair comparison?
Example A: Count both gates for the same five minutes.
Example B: Count one gate for twice as long.
questions.model: Count both gates for the same five minutes. Different observation durations can create an artificial difference.

questions.prompt: How much did the count change from 09:00 to 09:05?
lines: Fictional queue count: at 09:00, 9 people; at 09:05, 14; at 09:10, 11. Observer A counts people waiting inside the barrier. Observer B also counts people walking past.
questions.model: It increased by 5. The subtraction compares the two counts.

questions.prompt: Does the highest queue count prove slow service?
lines: Fictional queue count: at 09:00, 9 people; at 09:05, 14; at 09:10, 11. Observer A counts people waiting inside the barrier. Observer B also counts people walking past.
questions.model: No. More arrivals can also enlarge a queue. Measure arrivals and service times before explaining the cause.

blocks.title: Evidence hearing · Turn an observation into an investigable exhibit label
lines: Station 1: Give a verdict using the supplied evidence.
A partner challenges one claim; respond by distinguishing what is supported from what is still unknown.

Review case: Which label could guide a real school investigation? Proposed answer: “Our path: the best path in the world.”. Method note: An exhibit label needs more than a name. “Shaded bench: built seat beneath a tree; is it cooler here at noon?” identifies a feature, a connection and a question that measurements could answer.

questions.prompt: How can one school place involve both people and nature?
questions.model: A garden has plants and soil, while people plant and water it.

questions.prompt: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
questions.model: No. Use a compass or a map’s north arrow; a ruler measures length.

questions.prompt: Does a long queue prove that service is slow?
questions.model: No. More arrivals could also increase the queue; count and time what happens.

questions.prompt: Which label could guide a real school investigation?
lines:
Which label could guide a real school investigation?
Example A: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil?
Example B: Our path: the best path in the world.
questions.model: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

questions.prompt: Which field note is checkable?
lines:
Which field note is checkable?
Example A: At 10:00, three bags were beside the west wall.
Example B: The room was popular.
questions.model: At 10:00, three bags were beside the west wall. Time, count and location let someone repeat the observation; popularity needs other evidence.

questions.prompt: A queue is longer at Gate X. What can a single count establish?
lines: A queue is longer at Gate X. What can a single count establish?
questions.model: More people were waiting there at that moment. A snapshot describes a moment; repeated timing would be needed to compare service.

questions.prompt: Explain one possible connection between them.
lines: Fictional field sketch: a river bank beside a car park. Proposed change: the bank is paved. No before-and-after measurements have been made.
questions.model: The proposed human action may change shade, infiltration or habitat. Describe the effect relevant to this source; it is a prediction until observations test it.

questions.prompt: Does the highest queue count prove slow service?
lines: Fictional queue count: at 09:00, 11 people; at 09:05, 16; at 09:10, 13. Observer A counts people waiting inside the barrier. Observer B also counts people walking past.
questions.model: No. More arrivals can also enlarge a queue. Measure arrivals and service times before explaining the cause.

questions.prompt: Does a pattern prove what caused it?
questions.model: No. A pattern supports a claim about distribution; a cause needs further evidence.

questions.prompt: Which source tests whether access attracts customers?

Example B: The shop's paint colour.
questions.model: A customer survey of travel mode and reason for visiting. Travel evidence addresses the proposed mechanism directly.

questions.prompt: A station opens in 2020; a shop opens in 2015. What is ruled out?
lines: A station opens in 2020; a shop opens in 2015. What is ruled out?

questions.prompt: Suggest a reason without claiming proof.

lines: Decode features using the supplied key.
Convert the ratio scale into metres per centimetre.
At 1:25,000, 2 cm is 500 m; at 1:250,000 it is 5 km. The latter covers more ground in the same page space, leaving less room for local detail. A larger denominator means a smaller map scale.

blocks.title: Worked example · Build the hill profile
lines: Plot height against horizontal distance.
Compare rise over the same distance.

Distance belongs on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical. Join points in distance order. Over equal horizontal intervals, the greatest rise is the steepest segment; high elevation alone does not decide steepness.

blocks.title: Design a counterexample · Distinguish detail from coverage
lines: Station 1: Create a changed case in which a tempting answer fails.
Show the original reasoning, change one condition and explain what must now be reconsidered.

Review case: Which usually allows more detail for a local walk? Proposed answer: “1:250,000.”. Method note: At 1:25,000, 2 cm is 500 m; at 1:250,000 it is 5 km. The latter covers more ground in the same page space, leaving less room for local detail. A larger denominator means a smaller map scale.

questions.prompt: How could we decode an unfamiliar map symbol?
questions.model: Read that map’s key; do not rely on colour or a guess.

questions.prompt: Is the highest hill always the steepest?
questions.model: No. Steepness depends on rise over horizontal distance, not summit height alone.

questions.prompt: Does a latitude such as 20°N identify one unique place?
questions.model: No. It identifies a line; longitude is also needed to locate a point.

questions.prompt: Which usually allows more detail for a local walk?
lines:
Which usually allows more detail for a local walk?
Example A: 1:25,000.
Example B: 1:250,000.
questions.model: 1:25,000. More paper space is available per unit of ground distance at 1:25,000.

questions.prompt: Can the lower hill have the steeper side?
lines: Can the lower hill have the steeper side?
questions.model: Yes, if height increases more quickly over horizontal distance. Elevation and gradient measure different things.

questions.prompt: Which quadrant contains 15°N, 25°W?
lines:
Which quadrant contains 15°N, 25°W?
Example A: North-west of the zero-line intersection.
Example B: South-east of the zero-line intersection.
questions.model: North-west of the zero-line intersection. N belongs to latitude; W belongs to longitude.

questions.prompt: What ground distance does 1 cm represent on A?
lines: Original classroom map key: P = parking, blue line = stream, dashed line = footpath. Map A scale 1:25,000; Map B scale 1:250,000. A dashed route measures 10 cm on A and crosses a stream.
questions.model: 25,000 cm = 250 m. Convert centimetres to metres.

questions.prompt: Move A to the opposite side of the prime meridian, keeping latitude.
lines: Coordinate sketch: A 45°N, 55°E; B 45°S, 55°E; C 45°N, 55°W. Equator = 0° latitude; prime meridian = 0° longitude.
questions.model: It becomes 45°N, 55°W: the location of C.

Contour: A line joining equal heights. Points on one contour have equal height.

Gradient: How steep a slope is. Compare rise with horizontal distance.

blocks.title: What is a perspective?
lines: A perspective is someone’s way of seeing an issue.
Ask: “What do they think? Why does it matter to them?”
Both pupils are talking about the same playground.
Sam values exercise and playing with friends.
Amina values quiet and being able to concentrate.
A perspective includes a view and the reasons behind it.

Review case: Which statement places Northern Ireland correctly? Proposed answer: “Part of Great Britain, east of England.”. blocks.title: Mistake clinic · Explain relief rainfall as a connected process
lines: Station 2: Find the error in the proposed answer.
Replace it, explain the misconception and write a clue that would help another pupil avoid it.

Review case: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal? Proposed answer: “The mountain creates the missing water.”. Method note: Moist air rises over high ground and cools. Condensation can form cloud and precipitation. Descending air on the other side may be drier; wind and moisture supply matter, so a mountain does not guarantee rain every day.

questions.model: Cardiff is in Wales, on the island of Great Britain. Wales is a country; Great Britain is an island containing Wales, England and Scotland.

questions.prompt: Explain how the mountain helps rain form
lines: Follow the moist air from the sea up the mountain.
Explain the chain: rises → cools → condenses → rain can fall.
questions.model: The mountain forces moist air to rise. As the air rises, it cools, so water vapour can condense into cloud droplets. When droplets grow large enough, rain can fall. The water comes from moisture in the air; the mountain does not create it.

blocks.title: Mistake clinic · Combine layers to answer a specific question
lines: Station 1: Find the error in the proposed answer.
Replace it, explain the misconception and write a clue that would help another pupil avoid it.

Review case: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone? Proposed answer: “That it moves between the mapped territories.”. Method note: For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys. Keep the layers separate until you ask how one route intersects both.
blocks.imageAlt: Human buildings and natural relief in an imagined landscape.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Mistake clinic · Compare weather measurements without calling them climate
lines: Station 2: Find the error in the proposed answer.
Replace it, explain the misconception and write a clue that would help another pupil avoid it.

Review case: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported? Proposed answer: “A always has the wetter climate.”. Method note: A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C. Rainfall in millimetres is a separate variable. One wet day is weather; climate needs records across many years, not just a larger number from one day.
blocks.imageAlt: One day’s weather compared with seasonal and long-term observations.

lines: Station 3: Find the error in the proposed answer.

Review case: A survey of 20 club volunteers has 15 cyclists. Which headline is justified? Proposed answer: “Three quarters of every town's residents cycle.”. Method note: If 9 of 12 respondents prefer cycling, report that proportion and identify the respondents. “Everyone cycles” is false even within the sample. Generalising to a country also needs a representative selection method.

questions.prompt: Do country boundaries and mountain ranges show the same information?
questions.model: No. Boundaries are political divisions; mountains show physical relief.

questions.prompt: Can one cold day tell us a place’s climate?
questions.model: No. Weather describes a short period; climate needs observations over many years.

questions.prompt: Can someone belong to more than one community?
questions.model: Yes. A person can share several interests or connections; overlapping groups must not be counted twice.

questions.prompt: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone?
lines: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone?
questions.model: That it climbs a mountain. A boundary describes jurisdiction, not a guaranteed change of height.

questions.prompt: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported?
lines: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported?
questions.model: A received 10 mm more rain today. The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern.

questions.prompt: A survey of 20 club volunteers has 15 cyclists. Which headline is justified?
lines:
A survey of 20 club volunteers has 15 cyclists. Which headline is justified?
Example A: 15 of 20 surveyed club volunteers cycle.
Example B: Three quarters of every town's residents cycle.
questions.model: 15 of 20 surveyed club volunteers cycle. The survey describes the selected respondents; coverage and selection limit wider claims.

questions.prompt: Which two features are physical?
lines: Map layers: country boundary for Scotland; approximate upland area labelled Scottish Highlands; river line labelled Thames. A city point is also marked. Colours and symbols are explained in the key.
questions.model: Scottish Highlands and Thames: relief and a river, rather than a country boundary.

questions.prompt: Can this show what every pupil at school prefers?
lines: Fictional club survey: 14 pupils like walking only, 10 like cycling only, 11 like both. Everyone surveyed likes at least one. The survey was conducted at an outdoor club.
questions.model: No. Outdoor-club respondents may not represent all pupils.

Teach the missing step · Combine layers to answer a specific question: Review case: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone? Proposed answer: “That it moves between the mapped territories.”. Method note: For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys. Keep the layers separate until you ask how one route intersects both.
Teach the missing step · Compare weather measurements without calling them climate: Review case: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported? Proposed answer: “A always has the wetter climate.”. Method note: A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C. Rainfall in millimetres is a separate variable. One wet day is weather; climate needs records across many years, not just a larger number from one day.
Teach the missing step · Write a headline that respects the sample: Review case: A survey of 20 club volunteers has 15 cyclists. Which headline is justified? Proposed answer: “Three quarters of every town's residents cycle.”. Method note: If 9 of 12 respondents prefer cycling, report that proportion and identify the respondents. “Everyone cycles” is false even within the sample. Generalising to a country also needs a representative selection method.

lines: Station 2: Create a changed case in which a tempting answer fails.
Show the original reasoning, change one condition and explain what must now be reconsidered.

Review case: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal? Proposed answer: “The mountain creates the missing water.”. lines: Station 1: Give a verdict using the supplied evidence.
A partner challenges one claim; respond by distinguishing what is supported from what is still unknown.

Review case: A new clinic cuts average travel time. What can be concluded directly? Proposed answer: “Every resident's quality of life is now best.”. Method note: If clinic travel drops from 40 to 15 minutes, access improves by 25 minutes. It does not follow that housing, air quality or every resident's health improved. Change the specific claim and retain the unknowns.

questions.prompt: Can income alone tell us how well people can live?
questions.model: No. Access to services, costs, environment and different needs also matter.

questions.prompt: Can a city have more than one function?
questions.model: Yes. Government, work, housing, culture and transport can be connected in one city.

questions.prompt: Can one shipment be both an export and an import?
questions.model: Yes. It leaves the sending country as an export and enters the receiving country as an import.

questions.prompt: A new clinic cuts average travel time. What can be concluded directly?
lines: A new clinic cuts average travel time. What can be concluded directly?
questions.model: Average access time improved. One improved indicator does not establish every outcome for every person.

questions.prompt: Which arrow label explains a city connection?
lines:
Which arrow label explains a city connection?
Example A: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum.
Example B: Station and museum are both words.
questions.model: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum. The first names the movement and its function.

questions.prompt: Which response directly moves goods around a closed port?
lines:
Which response directly moves goods around a closed port?
Example A: Use another available port and compare added cost.
Example B: Send the shop more emails only.
questions.model: Use another available port and compare added cost. Information can coordinate action, but goods need a usable physical route.

questions.prompt: Which offers the shorter clinic journey?
lines: Fictional neighbourhood A: average income 65 tokens, clinic 10 minutes away, no park. B: average income 80, clinic 35 minutes away, park nearby. These are averages and travel estimates, not descriptions of every resident.
questions.model: A by 25 minutes. A person needing frequent care may value this strongly.

questions.prompt: Does a port closure automatically stop online messages?
lines: Fictional trade: bicycles move from Country C to Country D. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.
questions.model: No. Different flows can use different networks.

List indicators, units and affected users. Ask what averages hide before ranking a whole place.
Teach the missing step · Trace a disruption through a network: Review case: A station closes but a bus route remains open. What should planners compare? Proposed answer: “Assume nobody can reach the area.”. Method note: A closed station removes one access point but not every city function. Trace an alternative route, count extra changes and identify who bears the cost. Visitors and commuters may experience different effects.
Teach the missing step · Track goods, people and information separately: Review case: A UK shop receives goods from another country. From the UK viewpoint, these are what? Proposed answer: “Exports.”. Method note: A shipment leaving A and entering B is an export for A and an import for B. A message may travel without the goods moving yet. Label the arrow type and whose viewpoint defines the trade word.

blocks.title: Words for today
lines: Deposition: Material being dropped. Melting ice releases its debris.
Till: Unsorted material deposited by ice. Clay, sand and boulders are mixed together.
Moraine: A build-up of debris carried or deposited by a glacier. Debris can build a ridge at an ice margin.

questions.prompt: Which pair best tests whether heavy use is affecting a path?

questions.prompt: Which measure describes pressure, and which describes condition?

questions.prompt: Will moving visitors automatically solve the problem?

questions.model: No. B may be sensitive or lack capacity. Monitor both routes.

Design a counterexample · Use river-network vocabulary correctly: Review case: Two streams join. What is the meeting point called? Proposed answer: “A watershed.”. Design a counterexample · Compare surface and underground pathways: Review case: After rainfall, must all water reach the river immediately? Proposed answer: “Yes; the cycle has no storage.”. lines: Meltwater: Water produced when ice melts. Melting ice feeds a stream.
Storage: Water held in a place or form. Ice holds water before it is released.
Water balance: The difference between water inputs and outputs. Inputs minus outputs change the store.
blocks.imageAlt: Ice stores water and releases meltwater into a valley.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Words for today
lines: Source: Where a river begins. A spring can begin a river.
Tributary: A smaller river joining another river. A smaller channel joins the main river.
Mouth: Where a river enters the sea or another water body. Follow flow to a lake, sea or other water body.
blocks.imageAlt: Tributaries joining a main river between watershed ridges.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Words for today
lines: Evaporation: Liquid water becoming water vapour. Energy helps liquid water become vapour.
Condensation: Water vapour becoming liquid droplets. Cooling vapour can form cloud droplets.
Precipitation: Water falling from clouds. Rain or snow returns water to land or sea.

questions.prompt: Does more meltwater today guarantee more water forever?
questions.model: No. A shrinking ice store may release more water now but cannot sustain that contribution indefinitely.

questions.prompt: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
questions.model: No. It means in the direction of river flow towards the mouth.

questions.prompt: When water evaporates, does it stop existing?
questions.model: No. Liquid water changes into water vapour and moves through the water cycle.

questions.prompt: Start 50, add 4, lose 9. What is the final store?
lines: Start 50, add 4, lose 9. What is the final store?
questions.model: 45 units. 50 + 4 - 9 = 45; losses leave the store.

questions.prompt: A pollutant enters at B on A → B → C. Which place is downstream?
lines:
A pollutant enters at B on A → B → C. Which place is downstream?
Example A: C.
Example B: A.
questions.model: C. Follow the indicated flow direction; a precise warning time needs more data.

questions.prompt: Which process turns water vapour into liquid droplets?
lines:
Which process turns water vapour into liquid droplets?
Example A: Condensation.
Example B: Infiltration.
questions.model: Condensation. Condensation changes state; infiltration is water entering the ground.

questions.prompt: How much water left the store during that period?
lines: Fictional glacier water store: starts 110 units; gains 11; loses 16. A second period has the same gain but 5 extra units lost. These are model units, not a forecast.
questions.model: 16 units. Outflow is different from the amount remaining.

questions.prompt: What is infiltration?
lines: A fictional water-cycle model follows water from a lake into air, then a cloud, rain, soil and a stream. Some water remains stored underground.
questions.model: Water entering the soil from the surface.

questions.prompt: Does river width alone tell us its discharge?
questions.model: No. Discharge also depends on cross-sectional area and flow velocity.

questions.prompt: Rain falls on opposite sides of a ridge separating two basins. What may happen?
lines: Rain falls on opposite sides of a ridge separating two basins. What may happen?
questions.model: It drains towards different rivers. The ridge can separate downhill flow paths.

questions.prompt: Is the watershed the same as the main river?
lines: A fictional basin has three tributaries joining a main river. A high ridge separates it from a neighbouring river system.
questions.model: No. The river is a flow channel; the watershed is a dividing boundary.

questions.prompt: Can rain just across the ridge feed a different river?
lines: A fictional basin has three tributaries joining a main river. A high ridge separates it from a neighbouring river system.
questions.model: Yes. Its surface drainage may go into the neighbouring basin.

lines: Today’s task: Sediment journey
You will make a sediment storyboard.
Use remove, carry and lay down for the three actions.

Explain how flow and particle properties affect settling.

blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Words for today
lines: Erosion: Wearing away and removing material. Water removes material from a bank.
Transportation: Moving sediment. A pebble is carried downstream.
Deposition: Dropping sediment. A pebble settles as flow conditions change.
blocks.imageAlt: River sediment transported in different positions relative to the bed.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Rivers erode, transport and deposit
lines: Erosion removes material.
Transport moves it; deposition leaves it behind.
blocks.imageAlt: River sediment is removed, transported or deposited; explain the action shown.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Erosion has different mechanisms
lines: Water can remove weakened material.
Carried particles can abrade the bed and banks.
blocks.imageAlt: River sediment is removed, transported or deposited; explain the action shown.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Particles move in different ways
lines: Large particles can roll; smaller ones can bounce.
Fine material can be suspended; dissolved material travels in solution.
blocks.imageAlt: River sediment is removed, transported or deposited; explain the action shown.
blocks.imageCaption: Imagined concept illustration · exact case information is supplied separately.

blocks.title: Deposition depends on carrying capacity
lines: Slower or changed flow can release sediment.
Different materials settle under different conditions.

blocks.title: Worked example · Sediment journey
lines: Use remove, carry and lay down for the three actions.
Link the actions in a sediment journey.

Erosion removes material, transport moves it and deposition leaves it behind. The same grain can experience all three at different places or times. Attach action verbs to a grain's story rather than just name locations.

cards.back: No. Transport moves material; deposition leaves it behind when conditions change.

cards.front: I can distinguish removing, moving and dropping sediment.
cards.back:
Today’s task: Sediment journey
You will make a sediment storyboard.
Use remove, carry and lay down for the three actions.

Erosion: Wearing away and removing material. Water removes material from a bank.
Transportation: Moving sediment. A pebble is carried downstream.
Deposition: Dropping sediment. A pebble settles as flow conditions change.

Erosion removes material.
Transport moves it; deposition leaves it behind.

Water can remove weakened material.
Carried particles can abrade the bed and banks.

Large particles can roll; smaller ones can bounce.
Fine material can be suspended; dissolved material travels in solution.

Slower or changed flow can release sediment.
Different materials settle under different conditions.

Use remove, carry and lay down for the three actions.
Link the actions in a sediment journey.
Erosion removes material, transport moves it and deposition leaves it behind. The same grain can experience all three at different places or times. Attach action verbs to a grain's story rather than just name locations.

The river carries the material downstream or along the bed.

cards.back: No. It remains in a deposit and may be moved again later.

blocks.title: Six landform process cards
lines: Choose three cards: draw and explain one erosion feature, one bend feature and one deposition feature.
Partners cover the other three, then teach each other.

Waterfall: step/drop, undercutting and collapse. Gorge: steep-sided valley left as a waterfall retreats. Meander: bend migration. Oxbow lake: isolated cut-off bend. Floodplain: valley floor built partly by flood deposits. Natural levee: raised bank of deposited sediment.

questions.prompt: Can one low-tide depth establish safe passage at every time?

lines: Keep rainfall the same when comparing surfaces.
Account for infiltration and runoff.

lines: Flood: Water covering normally dry land. Water spreads beyond the channel.
Runoff: Water flowing over the land surface. Water moves across a paved surface.
Infiltration: Water soaking into the ground. Water enters pores in soil.

lines: Cause: A factor contributing to an event. Prolonged rain adds water to a basin.

blocks.title: Mistake clinic · Control one variable in a runoff experiment
lines: Station 1: Find the error in the proposed answer.
Replace it, explain the misconception and write a clue that would help another pupil avoid it.

Review case: Rain is 40 units and infiltration 25%. How much is model runoff? Proposed answer: “10 units.”. Method note: In a simplified 20-unit rainfall trial, 60% infiltration means 12 infiltrate and 8 run off. At 30%, 6 infiltrate and 14 run off. Keep rainfall fixed to isolate infiltration's effect; the model omits storage and timing.

blocks.title: Mistake clinic · Match a response to the flood mechanism
lines: Station 2: Find the error in the proposed answer.
Replace it, explain the misconception and write a clue that would help another pupil avoid it.

Review case: A local drain is blocked after rain. What directly addresses that blockage? Proposed answer: “Assume a distant tidal barrier clears it.”. Method note: A tidal barrier addresses incoming high water at its protected location; it does not remove every upstream rainfall or drainage problem. Warnings help preparation, while drainage work addresses a different pathway.

lines: Station 3: Find the error in the proposed answer.

Method note: With 50 tokens, a 10-token warning system and 30-token storage area cost 40, leaving 10. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water.
